newsitem.title: USA: Republican money advantage helped keep Congress.
newsitem.headline: Republican money advantage helped keep Congress.

text.p: A large edge in corporate and private political donations helped the Republicans keep control of Congress in last November's elections, according to an independent report issued Friday.

The report by Citizen Action, a political watchdog group which monitors campaign fundraising, said the Republican advantage was concentrated in significant battleground races and proved decisive in allowing the party to maintain a narrow majority in the House of Representatives.
"This report confirms again what most Americans believe -- that, more and more, elections are determined by the highest bidder," said Citizen Action director Ira Arlook.
In recent days, newspapers have reported that Republican leaders have put pressure on corporate interests to stop hedging their bets by giving money both to the Democrats and the Republicans.

The Citizen Action report said that where Democrats and Republicans enjoyed rough parity in their financial resources, Democrats tended to win. But when Republicans mustered a large money edge, they almost invariably won.
In the 10 closest House races won by Democrats, the Democratic candidates raised on average $94,000 less than their Republican opponents.
In 10 close races where Republicans won by two percent or less, they raised an average of $370,000 or 56 percent more than their opponents.
Corporate special interest political action committees contributed $97.8 million to Republican congressional candidates and $41.4 million to Democrats.
Large individual donors gave $197 million to Republican candidates and $132 million to Democrats.
